metadata.working_title: 68-year-old woman, chest pain at her husband's funeral, brought in by EMS
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: There's an elephant on my chest and I can't get my breath.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy, apical type, with dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and cardiogenic shock. It cannot be told apart from an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction before angiography, so it is treated as one in the emergency department. The angiogram, which the learner sees only in the debrief, shows no obstructive coronary disease and apical ballooning.
learning_objectives: Treat chest pain with ST elevation as an acute coronary occlusion whatever the story: ECG early, aspirin, and activation of the catheterization laboratory.
Do not let an emotional trigger or a family's explanation downgrade a dangerous ECG.
Before treating cardiogenic shock, listen to the heart and put a probe on it, because a murmur and an echo can reverse the plan.
Recognize dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction: a new harsh systolic murmur, a base that squeezes hard and an apex that does not move.
In outflow obstruction avoid nitrates, inotropes and diuretics, and give cautious fluid when the lungs are clear and a vasoconstrictor without inotropic effect.
Call cardiology early when the pressure falls, and stop a drug that is making the patient worse.
metadata.teaching_frame: Two reflexes are wrong for this patient and both feel right. The first is to believe the story: she has just buried her husband, so it must be grief. The second is to treat a weak heart with a low pressure the usual way, with an inotrope. The case is hard on purpose, and the cardiologist is there to help the moment the learner asks.

care_setting.label: Urban academic emergency department with a catheterization laboratory
care_setting.detail: Adult emergency department. Interventional cardiology on call and a catheterization laboratory available at any hour, which is why thrombolysis is the wrong choice here. Intensive care and mechanical circulatory support on site.

arrival.line: Brought in by EMS from a funeral reception. Her daughter came in the ambulance.

patient.background:
Retired schoolteacher. Treated high blood pressure and high cholesterol, on amlodipine and atorvastatin. No known heart disease and no murmur ever mentioned. Never smoked. Father had a heart attack at 70. No allergies. Gallbladder removed twenty years ago. Three children. Walks two miles a day and had a routine checkup in the spring.

Her husband of 41 years died five days ago. She has barely eaten or drunk since. At the reception after his funeral, about an hour ago, she developed crushing central chest pain going into her left arm and jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. Her daughter thinks it is grief and exhaustion and says so to everyone.
patient.presenting_appearance: A woman in a black dress, sitting upright on the stretcher, pale and sweating, one fist against her breastbone. She answers in short sentences. Her daughter is beside her holding her other hand.
patient.ems_handover_text: Sixty-eight year old woman, crushing central chest pain for about an hour, came on at her husband's funeral reception. Radiates to the left arm and jaw, with sweating and nausea. Hypertension and high cholesterol. Rate 115, pressure 96 over 60 with us. We gave nothing, she didn't have a line when we left. Daughter thinks it's stress.
patient.arrival_handover: Sixty-eight year old lady, chest pain for about an hour, came on at her husband's funeral. Her daughter's with her and says she's been in a state all week.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 2.3. Two sentences, 29 words. No vital sign, no past history, no medication, no pertinent negative. It carries the misleading frame on purpose: the crew repeats the daughter's explanation, as crews do.

phase_notes.count_justification: Four clinical phases and one terminal: arrival, the obstruction declaring itself, worse on the wrong treatment or none, and steadied. No halted phase and no arrest.
phase_notes.the_scripted_drop: The arrival phase ends at 180 seconds whatever is done, so every learner meets outflow obstruction. A learner with fluid and a vasoconstrictor already running goes straight to steadied.
phase_notes.the_cardiologist: On the directing physician's instruction the nurse recommends cardiology twenty seconds after the pressure falls (sixty in the default mode), the cardiologist gives the plan outright, and ninety seconds after being called takes over and steadies her.
phase_notes.no_halted_phase: On the directing physician's decision she cannot die and nothing halts the case. No action is tagged harmful, so there is no halted phase and no arrest.

phases.label: Chest pain with ST elevation, borderline pressure
phases.clinical_description: In pain, sweating, talking. Anterior ST elevation. Pressure 96 over 60 with a new harsh systolic murmur and clear lungs. The obstruction is already there and has not yet declared itself.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, narrow complexes. The report gives 1 mm of ST elevation in lead II, so the monitor lead is drawn with 0.1 mV. Model output.

transitions.narration: She's worse since that inotrope went in. Her rate is up, her pressure is down and she's confused.
transitions.debrief_note:
An inotrope made her worse within seconds. Her ventricle is weak at the apex and overactive at the base. Driving it harder narrowed the outflow tract further, and the faster rate left it less time to fill.

This is the reflex the case exists to interrupt. A low pressure with a poor ejection fraction usually gets an inotrope. Here the murmur was the warning that the usual answer was wrong.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Catecholamine inotropes worsen dynamic outflow obstruction by physiological reasoning and consensus. The size and speed are teaching choices. Model output.

transitions.narration: Her pressure has dropped since that vasodilator and her rate is up. She says she feels faint.
transitions.debrief_note:
A nitrate dropped her pressure. Nitrates lower the filling of the heart and the resistance it pumps against. In outflow obstruction a smaller, emptier ventricle obstructs more.

The warning was there before the drug: a pressure of 96 over 60 and a new murmur. A borderline pressure is a reason to hold a nitrate in any chest pain patient.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. She would have reached this phase anyway at 180 seconds. The nitrate brings it forward and gives it a cause. Model output.

transitions.when: flag inotrope_given set OR flag nitrate_given set
transitions.narration: Her pressure has fallen and her rate is up. She's gone gray and I can hear that murmur from here.
transitions.debrief_note: Her pressure fell at the moment this illness makes it fall. A nitrate or an inotrope had been given seconds before, and what that drug does to an obstructed outflow tract is described under the drug.
transitions.author_rationale: Added on 7 October 2026 to close a race between timed rules (authoring 15.4). A nitrate or an inotrope given less than ten seconds before the scripted fall, with fluid and a vasoconstrictor already running, used to send her straight to steadied with the wrong drug's effect on the monitor and a nurse line that said her pressure was holding. Now the fall happens first and the wrong drug acts from the obstructed phase, as it does at every other time. Same clock as the two rules below, so the owner's 180 seconds is unchanged. A positive guard, so it asks for no prompt. Model output.

transitions.when: flag fluids_given set AND flag vasoconstrictor_running set
transitions.narration: Her pressure is holding on the vasoconstrictor and her rate has come down.
transitions.debrief_note: The fall in pressure that this illness produces arrived and was already treated, because fluid and a vasoconstrictor were running. Acting on the murmur and the echo before the pressure fell is the best version of this case.
transitions.author_rationale: Same clock as the unguarded rule below, so the obstruction declares itself at one moment whatever was done. Model output.

transitions.narration: Her pressure has fallen and her rate is up. She's gone gray and I can hear that murmur from here.
transitions.debrief_note:
Her pressure fell without anything being given. This is the outflow obstruction declaring itself, and it is not a mistake on your part.

It is the decision point of the case. She has a weak ventricle, ST elevation and a low pressure, which looks like cardiogenic shock from a large infarct. The murmur and the echo say something more specific, and the treatment is different.
transitions.author_rationale: Scheduled natural history, so that every learner meets the obstruction. Three minutes of case clock. Outflow obstruction is the minority course in takotsubo and this case makes it happen every time. A teaching choice, approved in outline by the directing physician. Model output for the number.
transitions.unguarded_rationale: Without this rule a careful learner who never gives a nitrate or an inotrope never meets the third learning goal. The phase it leads to is recoverable, the nurse recommends cardiology twenty seconds after it in easy mode and sixty seconds after it in the default mode, and the cardiologist gives the plan and will take over.

phases.label: Outflow obstruction, hypotensive
phases.clinical_description: Mean arterial pressure 61. Gray, lightheaded, still talking. The murmur is louder. Fluid and a vasoconstrictor together get her out. An inotrope makes her worse.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, narrow complexes. The report gives 1 mm of ST elevation in lead II, so the monitor lead is drawn with 0.1 mV. Model output.

transitions.narration: She's worse since that inotrope went in. Her rate is up, her pressure is down and she's confused.
transitions.debrief_note:
An inotrope made her worse. The base of her heart was already squeezing hard into a narrow outflow tract. More contractility and a faster rate narrowed it further.

Stop the drug. Then give a small fluid bolus and a vasoconstrictor with no inotropic effect.
transitions.author_rationale: As for the same rule on arrival. Model output.

transitions.when: flag fluids_given set AND flag vasoconstrictor_running set
transitions.narration: That's working. Her pressure is up, her rate is down and the murmur is softer.
transitions.debrief_note:
Fluid and a vasoconstrictor opened the outflow tract. A fuller ventricle and a higher resistance to pump against hold the obstruction apart, and the slower rate gives the heart time to fill.

This is the reverse of the usual plan for a weak heart. It applies to obstruction specifically, and it rests on physiology and expert consensus, not trials. She also had clear lungs. With pulmonary edema the fluid would be wrong.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Ten seconds compresses a titration of several minutes. Model output.

transitions.narration: Cardiology is at the bedside and has taken over. They've given a small fluid bolus and have a vasoconstrictor running. Her pressure is up and her rate is down.
transitions.debrief_note:
Cardiology came to the bedside and took over. They stopped anything with inotropic effect, gave a small fluid bolus because her lungs were clear, and started a pure vasoconstrictor.

Calling for help was the right move and it is what you would do. The reasoning to take from it: the base of her heart is squeezing hard into a narrowed outflow tract. Anything that makes the heart squeeze harder or faster, or empties it, tightens the obstruction. Filling it and raising the resistance it pumps against opens it.
transitions.author_rationale: Added on Aakash Setty's instruction of 6 October 2026: the cardiologist can take over and help, because this is a hard case. Ninety seconds after a call that is made, or was already made, when the pressure is low. A delayed consequence of the learner's own action, so the five-second floor applies. Ninety seconds leaves a learner who wants to act on the cardiologist's advice time to do it first. The clock belongs to one phase: a call made on arrival starts counting again when the pressure falls. Model output for the number.

transitions.when: NOT flag fluids_given set OR NOT flag vasoconstrictor_running set
transitions.narration: She's getting worse. Her rate is up, her pressure is down and she's not making sense.
transitions.debrief_note:
Her outflow tract stayed obstructed and her output kept falling. The base of her heart was squeezing hard into a narrowed outflow tract, and a ventricle that cannot empty past the obstruction supplies less blood to the brain and to the heart itself. The fast rate left it less time to fill, and an emptier ventricle obstructs more.

A small fluid bolus and a vasoconstrictor with no inotropic effect, given together, would have opened it. Either one alone was not enough.

If you were unsure what to do, that is reasonable. This is a hard presentation. Calling cardiology was always available, and the nurse suggested it.
transitions.author_rationale: Deterioration on inaction. The nurse recommends cardiology at 20 seconds, fluid at 45 and a vasoconstrictor at 60. In the default mode those are 60, 135 and 180 seconds, so all three are spoken before this rule fires at 240 (authoring 7.4). Four minutes is a drafting judgment.

tag_vocabulary.note: Harmful is not used. See phase_notes.no_halted_phase.

flag_namespace_note: Flags are permanent. An inotrope that has been stopped is inotrope_given with inotrope_stopped, and 'active' is the first without the second. Restarting a stopped inotrope has no further effect, which is a limit of the tool. vasoconstrictor_running is set by phenylephrine, vasopressin and norepinephrine.

prompt.text: She's not on a monitor yet. Do you want her hooked up?

case_actions.debrief_note: Nothing shows until the monitor is on. Her pressure of 96 over 60 is the number that should make you careful with everything you give for the pain.
A line comes before any intravenous drug, and she will need several.
A second line is worth having in anyone who may need a vasoactive infusion.

prompt.text: Chest pain for an hour and no ECG yet. Do you want a twelve-lead?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A twelve-lead within ten minutes of arrival is the standard for chest pain. Hers shows anterior ST elevation, and that decides the pathway whatever the story is.

Takotsubo can produce exactly this tracing. Elevation centered on V2 to V5 and II with little reciprocal depression is the pattern described in takotsubo. No feature of the ECG separates it reliably from an occluded artery, so the tracing is acted on as an infarct. [UNVERIFIED: the ten-minute standard was written from memory of the STEMI guidelines. The ECG pattern is from Ghadri et al. 2018, read through a summarizing tool]

prompt.guard: (phase is presentation OR phase is steadied) AND study ecg_12_lead resulted
prompt.text: She has ST elevation and she hasn't had aspirin. Do you want it given?

case_actions.debrief_note: Aspirin is given for a suspected coronary occlusion as soon as the ECG shows one. It is cheap, safe here, and the diagnosis that would make it unnecessary is not available until after the angiogram.

case_actions.narration_override: Calling the cath lab activation now.

prerequisites.failure_message: The cath lab will want a twelve-lead before they call the team in. Do you want one now?
The twelve-lead is still printing. The cath lab will want to see it before they call the team in.

prompt.text: That ECG has ST elevation across the front. Do you want me to activate the cath lab?

case_actions.debrief_note:
ST elevation with ongoing chest pain is a catheterization laboratory activation, and the usual target is the artery open within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Her daughter's explanation, the funeral and her grief do not change that. The laboratory takes the call once there is a twelve-lead to show them.

The angiogram is also the only test that makes the diagnosis here. It showed arteries without obstruction and a ventricle ballooning at the apex, which is takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Activating was right, and it was right for a patient who turned out not to have an infarct. [UNVERIFIED: the 90-minute target was written from memory of the STEMI guidelines]
Accepted as part of the infarct pathway. Many cardiologists want it given before the laboratory and some prefer to give it there. Not scored.
A second antiplatelet is the cardiologist's call before angiography. Not scored.
Fentanyl in a small dose is a reasonable way to treat her pain when a nitrate is the wrong choice. Opioids lower the pressure a little in some patients, so give it slowly and watch.
Morphine in a small dose is a reasonable way to treat her pain when a nitrate is the wrong choice. Opioids lower the pressure a little in some patients, so give it slowly and watch.
She is frightened and grieving, and a small dose is not wrong. It treats nothing that is causing the ST elevation, and feeling calmer is not the same as being safer.

vital_effects.while: NOT phase is presentation AND NOT phase is obstructed
vital_effects.note: Teaching choice. On arrival the nitrate moves her to the obstructed phase, and that phase's own numbers are the fall. The effect is guarded off there by name so the fall is counted once (authoring 16). A guard is read against the state now and cannot see where the drug was given, so a nitrate given in the obstructed phase also shows no further fall while she stays there. In worsening shock or once steadied it costs twelve points for what is left of two minutes.

case_actions.debrief_note:
Nitrates are a reflex for cardiac chest pain. They lower the filling of the heart and the resistance it pumps against. In outflow obstruction both make the obstruction worse, and her pressure was only 96 over 60 before it was given.

Guidelines say to hold nitrates with a systolic pressure under 90, or well below the patient's usual pressure, or with a fast heart rate. She is a treated hypertensive at 96 with a rate of 115. And a new murmur should be explained before preload is lowered. [UNVERIFIED: the nitrate thresholds were written from memory of the STEMI guidelines]

vital_effects.while: phase is steadied AND NOT flag inotrope_stopped set AND NOT flag cardiology_called set
vital_effects.note: Teaching choice. Once she is steadied an inotrope still costs her pressure. Guarded off once cardiology has been called, because a takeover stops the inotrope and a timed transition can set no flag. The cost: an inotrope started after a cardiology call shows nothing in the steadied phase.

vital_effects.while: phase is steadied AND NOT flag inotrope_stopped set AND NOT flag cardiology_called set

case_actions.debrief_note:
A low pressure with a poor ejection fraction usually gets an inotrope. In this patient the base of the ventricle is overactive and is squeezing the outflow tract shut. More contractility and a faster rate tighten it, and the pressure falls further.

The murmur was the clue that her shock had a mechanical cause. When a treatment makes the patient worse, stop it. Dobutamine, epinephrine and dopamine all count as the same act here.

Avoiding catecholamine inotropes in takotsubo with outflow obstruction rests on physiology and expert consensus. There are no trials. [UNVERIFIED: Ghadri et al., International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome, part II, Eur Heart J 2018]

vital_effects.note: Teaching choice. Stopping the inotrope alone gives back part of the pressure. The phase changes when fluid and a vasoconstrictor are added.

prompt.guard: phase is shock_worse AND NOT flag inotrope_stopped set
prompt.text: That inotrope is not helping her. Do you want it stopped?

case_actions.debrief_note: Stopping a drug that is making the patient worse is the first step of the rescue. It gives back part of the pressure she lost, and she then still needs fluid and a vasoconstrictor.

Fluid is the unusual part of this plan. A weak heart with a low pressure usually does not get fluid. She got it because her lungs were clear, her neck veins were flat, she was dry, and a fuller ventricle holds the outflow tract open.

prompt.text: Her pressure is still low. Do you want a pressor that squeezes the vessels without driving the heart, like phenylephrine?

case_actions.debrief_note:
Phenylephrine raises the resistance the heart pumps against and has no direct effect on contractility. It tends to slow the heart by reflex. In outflow obstruction all three of those help. Vasopressin does the same job without acting on catecholamine receptors and counts as the same act here.

This choice is borrowed from hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, where it is standard teaching. For takotsubo it is physiological reasoning and expert opinion. The 2018 consensus document recommends fluid and avoiding inotropes, nitrates and diuretics, and does not name a vasoconstrictor. Reviews that do name one prefer phenylephrine. Vasopressin is an extrapolation.

Phenylephrine adds load to a ventricle that is already weak, so it is right only while obstruction is the main problem. In takotsubo with shock and no obstruction the advice differs and mechanical support is often preferred. If drugs fail, the next step is mechanical support with a pump such as an Impella. A balloon pump lowers afterload and can worsen the obstruction. [UNVERIFIED: Ghadri et al. 2018 read through a summarizing tool. The reviews that name a vasoconstrictor are listed in TAKO-SEED.md without full citations]

vital_effects.note: Teaching choice: some beta effect, shown as a small rise in rate.

case_actions.debrief_note: Norepinephrine is mostly a vasoconstrictor with some effect on contractility and rate. It is the usual first vasopressor in shock. The case accepts it as the vasoconstrictor and treats it as the second choice. A drug with no beta effect is cleaner in obstruction. Some authors accept norepinephrine with careful titration and others consider it counterproductive.

case_actions.debrief_note:
A short-acting beta blocker slows the heart and reduces the force of the overactive base, which may relieve outflow obstruction. The consensus document says so, and it also says beta blockers are contraindicated in acute severe heart failure with a low ejection fraction and in hypotension.

She has both. The case treats a beta blocker as discouraged while her pressure is unsupported, and as neither right nor wrong once a vasoconstrictor is holding it. That later decision belongs to the cardiologist. [UNVERIFIED: Ghadri et al. 2018, read through a summarizing tool]

This is the second learning goal of the case. Before treating a low pressure in a patient with a weak heart, look at the heart. Hers shows an apex that does not contract and a base that contracts hard, and the mitral valve being drawn toward the septum.

That picture, with the murmur, means the low pressure has a mechanical cause that an inotrope makes worse. The same check applies in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in some anterior infarcts and in an over-diuresed small ventricle.

prompt_cap_recommendation.rationale: Four. On arrival: the monitor at 15 seconds, the ECG at 40, aspirin at 90 and the catheterization laboratory at 130. The last two fire only once the twelve-lead has resulted. With a low pressure: cardiology at 20, fluid at 45 and a vasoconstrictor at 60, which are the three the 240-second deterioration rests on and are the earliest. On an inotrope the stop prompt at 25 is the second of four, and the catheterization laboratory prompt at 130 is the one the cap drops. In the default mode every figure is tripled: 60, 135 and 180 seconds with a low pressure, all before 240. On arrival in the default mode only the monitor (45) and the ECG (120) prompts fire before the scripted fall at 180.

correct_disposition.label: Cardiac catheterization laboratory
correct_disposition.explanation:
She goes to the catheterization laboratory. She has ST elevation with chest pain, and nothing done in the emergency department can tell an occluded artery from takotsubo. The angiogram is both the treatment for one and the diagnosis of the other.

What happened next: her coronary arteries had no obstruction, and the ventriculogram showed the apex ballooning with a vigorous base. That is takotsubo cardiomyopathy. She went to cardiac intensive care on a vasoconstrictor and her ventricle recovered over the following weeks, as it usually does. It is not a benign illness: rates of shock and death in hospital are similar to those of a heart attack.

What the receiving team needs: the ECG, the murmur and the echo, what her pressure did, and which drugs helped and which made her worse.

alternative_dispositions.label: Intensive care unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She needs intensive care and she will get it, after the angiogram. Sending her there first leaves ST elevation with chest pain uninvestigated. Defensible only as the bed she goes to from the laboratory.

alternative_dispositions.label: Step-down or intermediate care with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She is on a vasoconstrictor with ST elevation and an ejection fraction of 30 percent. She needs an angiogram and then intensive care.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Telemetry watches a rhythm. It does not open an artery or run a vasoactive infusion.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation with serial troponins is for chest pain with a normal ECG. Hers shows ST elevation.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This is the outcome her daughter's explanation leads to. Grief does not cause ST elevation that can safely be sent home. Even when the cause turns out to be takotsubo, she has a failing ventricle and was in shock.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This hospital has a catheterization laboratory and cardiac intensive care.

correct_diagnosis.label: ST-elevation myocardial infarction
correct_diagnosis.explanation:
This is the right working diagnosis to hand over, and it is not what she had. Chest pain with anterior ST elevation is treated as an occluded coronary artery until an angiogram shows otherwise.

Her angiogram showed no obstruction and an apex that ballooned in systole: takotsubo cardiomyopathy, brought on by the death of her husband. Nothing available to you could have told the two apart. The emotional trigger, the very high natriuretic peptide and wall motion that crossed arterial territories all point toward takotsubo, and none of them is reliable enough to keep a patient out of the laboratory.

This case scores the working diagnosis you should have acted on. Naming takotsubo first is scored as defensible, because it turned out to be true and could only have been a guess.
correct_diagnosis._note: The scoring of the two diagnoses was decided by the directing physician, 6 October 2026.

additional_diagnoses.label: Cardiogenic shock
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her pressure fell with cold hands, a rising lactate and an ejection fraction of 30 percent. Saying so tells the laboratory to expect an unstable patient. Say with it that the shock was from outflow obstruction, which inotropes make worse, because that changes what they reach for.

additional_diagnoses.label: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Worth naming as a possibility beside the infarct. The trigger, the echo and the murmur all suggest it, and a team that has it in mind will do a ventriculogram and will not be surprised by clean arteries.

additional_diagnoses.label: Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
additional_diagnoses.explanation: Her low pressure came from the base of the ventricle squeezing the outflow tract shut. Naming it tells the next team why fluid and a vasoconstrictor helped, and why a nitrate or an inotrope would make her worse.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: This is what she had. As the primary diagnosis at handover it is a guess that happened to be right. It cannot be made before angiography, and a doctor who commits to it early may hold aspirin or delay the laboratory for a patient who has an occluded artery. Hand over the infarct and name this beside it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Cardiogenic shock
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True, and it describes her circulation without saying why. Name the cause first.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute coronary syndrome, unspecified
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Right family, too vague. ST elevation is the finding that sends her to the laboratory now, and the handover should say it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her ECG shows ST elevation in V2 to V5. That changes the urgency from hours to minutes.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Panic attack
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: This is her daughter's diagnosis. A panic attack does not cause ST elevation, a raised troponin, a new murmur or a ventricle that does not contract. Distress and serious disease often arrive together, and the first never excludes the second.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A good thought, because her murmur behaves like the murmur of hypertrophic obstruction and the treatment of the obstruction is the same. Her echo shows an apex that does not move, not a thick septum, and she has never had a murmur before.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Aortic dissection
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Worth a thought in any chest pain with a new murmur. Her pain is crushing and not tearing, her arm pulses are equal, her mediastinum is normal and the murmur is systolic. Most dissections have no murmur, and when one is present it is the diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Severe aortic stenosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A harsh systolic murmur with a low pressure makes this reasonable. The murmur of a fixed stenosis does not change with a Valsalva strain the way hers does. The echo settles it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Pulmonary embolism
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her right ventricle is normal on echo and her ECG shows precordial ST elevation with a left ventricle that is not contracting.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Myocarditis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: It can mimic an infarct and it can look like takotsubo. Angiography excludes coronary disease and does not separate the two. Cardiac MRI does, later. Either way she goes to the laboratory first.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute pericarditis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Pericarditis gives widespread ST elevation with PR depression and a rub, and it does not weaken the ventricle.

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: Every exam is tagged neutral, so the Physical score reads this list: the murmur, the clear lungs, the flat neck veins and the perfusion. Model judgment.
debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: The intended path passes through the obstructed phase, which arrives on a clock for every learner. A learner who has fluid and a vasoconstrictor running before it arrives goes straight to steadied.
debrief_configuration.trap_actions_note: Empty on purpose. Lorazepam was listed, and the debrief then printed it under things that looked reasonable and were not, while its own note says a small dose is not wrong.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: Chest pain with ST elevation is an occluded artery until an angiogram says otherwise. A funeral, a panic and a family's explanation do not change the pathway.
Before treating a low pressure in a weak heart, listen to it and look at it. A new systolic murmur can mean the usual treatment will make the patient worse.

In outflow obstruction the plan runs backwards: no nitrates, no inotropes, no diuretics. A small fluid bolus if the lungs are clear, and a vasoconstrictor that does not drive the heart. Avoiding those drugs and giving fluid is in the consensus document. The choice of vasoconstrictor is physiology and expert opinion.
When a treatment makes the patient worse, stop it. That is a decision, and it is often the hardest one in the room.
Call cardiology the moment the pressure falls in a patient with ST elevation. Asking for help early in a patient you do not fully understand is good practice.

Takotsubo cannot be diagnosed in the emergency department. The clues are an emotional or physical trigger, a very high natriuretic peptide and wall motion that crosses arterial territories. None of them keeps a patient out of the laboratory.
Outflow obstruction happens in a minority of patients with takotsubo. This case makes it happen every time so that you meet it.
